common_name: Roseum Crinum Lily (Deep Rose-Pink Hardy Crinum)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Roseum is a selected color form of the classic Crinum x powellii hybrid, chosen for flowers in a noticeably richer, deeper rose-pink than the soft pink typical of the species.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Roseum bears the same large clusters of trumpet-shaped flowers as its parent, Crinum x powellii, but in a saturated rose-pink rather than the softer blush of the species type, giving it more visual punch in mixed borders. It shares the same rock-solid constitution as other powellii selections, tolerating heat, humidity, brief flooding, and heavy clay with equal ease, and the huge bulb persists for decades once established. As with other crinums, flowering improves when the clump is left crowded and undisturbed for years, so divide only when vigor clearly declines.

common_name: Menehune Crinum (Dwarf Burgundy-Leaved Bog Crinum Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, with the neck at or just above the soil line; Menehune is a compact, deep burgundy-leaved crinum hybrid introduced from Hawaii and is unusual among crinums for tolerating standing water at the pond margin as well as ordinary border conditions.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in rich, consistently moist soil in full sun to light shade. Menehune is a dwarf crinum hybrid prized for its narrow, one- to two-inch-wide leaves that stay a deep, glossy burgundy-red all season rather than fading to green with age, forming a compact clump well under half the size of standard crinum selections. Clusters of large, deep pink, fragrant trumpet flowers rise on dark red stalks from early summer into fall, held well above the colorful foliage. Unlike most crinums it thrives in boggy soil and can be grown with its crown submerged a few inches at a pond margin, though it also performs well in an ordinary moist border, making it a versatile choice for rain gardens and water features.

common_name: Freckles Pineapple Lily (Dwarf Purple-Spotted Pineapple Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs after the soil has warmed in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Freckles is a dwarf, heavily spotted-leaf pineapple lily bred from Eucomis vandermerwei parentage and is notably more cold-hardy than most eucomis selections.

directions: Plant bulbs about three inches deep after danger of frost has passed, in rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in the hottest climates. Freckles forms a low, vigorous clump of dark green, wavy-margined leaves that are heavily speckled and flushed with purple, an ornamental feature on its own well before the dark purple flower spikes appear in midsummer, each topped with the small, starry blooms and pineapple-like leafy tuft typical of the genus. Bred from Eucomis vandermerwei stock, it is noticeably more compact and considerably hardier than many other pineapple lily selections, tolerating winters well beyond the usual eucomis comfort zone when given a deep mulch. It is an excellent front-of-border or container plant where its spotted foliage can be appreciated up close, and it draws bees and hummingbirds while in bloom.

planting.note: Plant bulbs, or divisions 'in the green' just after flowering, in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Trym was the first of the distinctive 'pagoda' shaped snowdrops, its outer petal segments elongating and curving upward as the flower matures.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Trym is a landmark snowdrop cultivar among collectors, notable for its long, tapering outer petal segments, each marked with a fat green sickle-shaped smudge, which start flat and curl gracefully upward within days of opening to give the nodding flower a distinctive pagoda-like silhouette unlike any older snowdrop cultivar. The inner segments carry a neat, symmetrical green marking that complements the outer pattern. It multiplies at a steady, moderate pace typical of plicatus-type snowdrops and is best divided immediately after flowering while the foliage is still green, making a striking addition to a shaded winter border or collector's trough.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Zwanenburg is the classic large-flowered ivory-white form of the popular hybrid spider lily, prized for its heavy fragrance and abundant summer bloom.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Zwanenburg produces showy umbels of up to five large, richly scented, ivory-white flowers with a scalloped central cup and six extremely narrow, spidery, spreading petals, opening over an extended period in mid to late summer above strappy, dark green foliage. It is the archetypal white-flowered counterpart to yellow-flowered sister selections like 'Sulphur Queen,' sharing the same easy care and heavy evening fragrance that draws moths and other pollinators at dusk. Bulbs slowly form offsets to build an expanding clump, and plants benefit from a dry winter mulch in the cooler end of their range, with best performance where summers are long, warm, and humid.

common_name: Martinez Rain Lily (Large Pink Argentine Habranthus)
subcategory: large-flowered South American rain lily bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; native to northern Argentina, Martinez rain lily flowers in flushes after late-summer rainfall, its large light-pink blooms held near horizontal in the characteristic Habranthus pose.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Martinez rain lily produces large, light pink, cup-shaped flowers with a contrasting dark green-to-purple base, held just above horizontal on sturdy scapes rather than strictly upright, giving the blooms a distinctively poised, outward-facing look. Native to open grasslands of northern Argentina, it responds to the shift from summer heat into early fall rain with a quick, showy flush of bloom that continues intermittently into October. Clumps are drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once established, needing only regular moisture through the growing season and a well-drained site to avoid bulb rot over winter.

common_name: Mini-Cherry Rain Lily (Dwarf Peachy-Pink Habranthus Cultivar)
subcategory: dwarf South American rain lily bulb

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mini-Cherry is a compact selection of Habranthus martinezii forming tight, vigorous clumps well under a foot tall, ideal for edging and container culture.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun. Mini-Cherry is a dwarf, densely clumping selection of Habranthus martinezii, bearing the same light peachy-pink, near-horizontal cup-shaped flowers with a dark purple base as the species, but on a plant scaled down to tidy eight-inch clumps rather than the taller, looser habit of the wild type. It flowers in flushes triggered by late-summer and early-fall rainfall, blooming reliably a few days after a heavy soaking. Its small, vigorous habit makes it especially well suited to rock gardens, border edges, and containers where the larger species types would sprawl, and like other habranthus it is drought-tolerant and easy-care once established in well-drained soil.

common_name: Traub's Rain Lily (Tall White Texas Rain Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; Traub's rain lily is native to the coastal plains of south Texas and northeastern Mexico, where it produces the tallest flower stalks of any Zephyranthes species and blooms in flushes after summer and fall rain events.

directions: Plant bulbs in well-drained, sandy loam soil in full sun. Traub's rain lily produces erect, salverform, white flowers, sometimes faintly tinged pink, on the tallest stalks of any commonly grown Zephyranthes species, with slender, often reflexed tepals and equal, fascicled stamens giving each bloom a crisp, star-like form. Native to open coastal-plain fields and sandy soils of south Texas and northeastern Mexico, it responds to rainfall with quick, synchronized flushes of bloom from midsummer through fall, later into the season than most other Gulf Coast rain lilies. The narrow, dull-green grassy foliage stays low and unobtrusive between bloom cycles, and once established the bulbs are extremely drought-tolerant, needing no supplemental water beyond natural rainfall.

common_name: Rosea Surprise Lily (Pink-and-Blue Hybrid Spider Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this natural hybrid between Lycoris radiata and Lycoris sprengeri sends up leafless flower stalks in mid- to late summer, well before its fall foliage appears.

directions: Plant bulbs with the neck at or just below soil level in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Lycoris x rosea is a naturally occurring hybrid between the fall-blooming red spider lily and the cold-hardy rose surprise lily, combining traits of both parents into flowers intermediate in form and color: narrow, more dissected magenta-to-pink tepals, each tipped in an unexpected streak of bright blue, clustered atop bare stalks from mid-July into late August depending on the individual clone. As with its parents, the strap-like foliage emerges in fall after bloom, overwinters as a low green rosette, and dies back by early summer, so it pairs well with later-emerging perennials that can screen the dormant gap. Once settled, clumps are best left undisturbed for several years, since flowering improves as the bulbs become slightly congested.
